title: SOLID Principles: Violation and Fix
summary: Quick revision notes on the five SOLID principles, each with a concrete violation and its fix, plus the trade-offs and mistakes that matter in practice.

chapters.title: SOLID Mental Model
points: SOLID = five class-design rules that keep code easy to change: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP
Core goal: a change in one requirement should touch one place, not ripple across many
Smell to principle map: giant class → SRP, growing if/else on type → OCP, subclass that throws → LSP, unused methods → ISP, `new` of concrete deps → DIP
Principles are guidelines for managing change, not laws: apply them when a real change pressure appears
Interview Point: Why does SOLID exist? Which smell maps to which principle? When is applying it overkill?

chapters.title: Single Responsibility and Open/Closed
points: SRP: a class has one reason to change, meaning one actor/stakeholder owns it
SRP violation: `Invoice` has calculateTotal(), saveToDb() and printPdf(), so tax, DB and layout changes all edit one class
SRP fix: split into `Invoice` (data and totals), `InvoiceRepository` (persistence) and `InvoicePrinter` (output)
OCP: open for extension, closed for modification; add behavior by adding code, not editing tested code
OCP violation: `area(shape)` uses if/elif on shape type, so every new shape edits the function; fix: `Shape` interface with `area()` and each shape implements it (polymorphism)
Interview Point: What is a 'reason to change'? How does OCP differ from SRP? Which pattern implements OCP (Strategy/polymorphism)? When is OCP premature?

chapters.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
points: LSP: any subtype must be usable wherever its base type is expected without breaking correctness
Contract rules: subtype may not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, or break base invariants
Violation: `Square extends Rectangle` overrides setWidth to also set height, so `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4)` expects area 20 but gets 16
Violation: `Penguin extends Bird` with fly() that throws, so callers of Bird.fly() crash

Fix: model by behavior, not 'is-a' wording: separate `Flyer` interface, or make Rectangle and Square independent `Shape` implementations; Interview Point: How do you detect an LSP break? Why does Square/Rectangle fail? What is a precondition vs postcondition?

chapters.title: Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion
points: ISP: no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use; prefer many small role interfaces
ISP violation: `Worker` interface has work() and eat(), so `Robot` must implement eat() as a no-op or throw; fix: split into `Workable` and `Eatable`
DIP: high-level modules depend on abstractions, not on low-level concrete classes; both depend on the interface
DIP violation: `OrderService` does `self.db = MySQLDatabase()` inside, so it cannot be tested or swapped; fix: define `Database` interface and inject it via the constructor
DIP is the principle, dependency injection is the technique, an IoC container is a tool; Interview Point: ISP vs SRP? DIP vs DI? How does DIP make unit testing easier?

chapters.title: Common SOLID Mistakes
points: Over-splitting: one-method classes everywhere makes code hard to follow; split only on a real second reason to change
Interface per class with exactly one implementation and no test seam is noise, not DIP
Inheritance used for code reuse instead of substitutability causes LSP breaks; prefer composition
Switch on type in only one place, with no new types expected, does not need OCP refactoring (rule of three)

Fat 'Manager' or 'Util' classes and `new` inside constructors are the top real-world violations to spot in review; Interview Point: Can you over-apply SOLID? Composition vs inheritance for LSP? How do you spot SRP issues in review?

chapters.title: SOLID Cheat Sheet
points: SRP: one reason to change, one actor; smell is a class doing DB plus logic plus output; fix by splitting responsibilities
OCP: extend without editing; smell is if/elif on type; fix with polymorphism or Strategy
LSP: subtype is substitutable; smell is override that throws or changes semantics; fix by composition or smaller interfaces
ISP: small role interfaces; smell is empty or throwing method implementations; fix by splitting the interface
DIP: depend on abstractions and inject them; smell is `new Concrete()` inside a service; fix with constructor injection
Interview Point: Recite SOLID with one smell each. Which principle is hardest to apply? Which two overlap most?
